newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FOCUS - Bulgaria risks hyper-inflation after float.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bulgaria risks hyper-inflation after float.

text.p: Economists on Monday urged further market liberalisation as the only way to avoid a plunge into hyper-inflation following the decision of Bulgaria's central bank to lift administrative controls on interest rates.
The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) on Friday warned politicians that it alone could not contain the grave financial crisis and abandoned controls on interest rates from Monday.

"Any liberalisation of the market will help clear the imbalances accumulated in the economy through previous inadequate administration and prepare it for introduction of a currency board," said macro-economic expert Mariela Nenova.

A political deadlock created by the refusal of the ruling former communists to agree to opposition calls for early elections has delayed talks on strict monetary measures designed to haul the country out of its economic problems.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposed the implementation of a currency board last year to halt the fall in value of the national currency, the lev, and restore confidence in ailing local banks.
The system requires levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank.
The BNB said on Friday it was replacing its main interest rate with the average weighted effective monthly yield of short-term treasury bill auctions held by the finance ministry.
"As the market rate was traditionally higher, the BNB decision signals a hidden rate hike. An official one would have produced more panic," Nenova told Reuters.
The State Savings Bank raised its annual interest rate on deposits to 360 percent, compared with the BNB's previous 180 percent.
"The new rates will inevitably be higher and fuel inflation," said Galina Dimitrova, chief economist of the Bulgarian Investment Bank.

Economists said last week that Bulgaria's economy had plunged into hyper-inflation for the first time. The monthly inflation rate for January was expected to hit 50 percent after inflation for the first 15 days of the month ran to 30.8 percent.
Panic-stricken Bulgarians rushed on Saturday to stock up on food as government officials advised them to spend their money as soon as possible to avoid losses caused by the lev's rapid depreciation.
Shops have closed as shopkeepers fear to stock up with goods that may change in price within hours.
The lev dipped to new lows of 950 to the dollar on Monday amid expectations of further political instability. The BNB fixed the currency at 813.87 for Monday, down from Friday's 731.71.

"The economy now is unbalanced and only full liberalisation of the market will allow it to find a new balance. If the currency board is introduced at that moment, then it will have a healing effect," said Nenova.
She said that only full liberalisation of prices accompanied by urgent structural reform would halt the crisis.
Current price controls on electricity rates, rail tickets and other goods and services can no longer be adjusted to the lev's volatility and will only increase deficits, she said.
The IMF had said it was prepared to renew talks with a credible government capable of implementing an approved reform programme.
President Petar Stoyanov is expected to ask the ruling Bulgarian Socialist Party, largely composed of ex-communists, to form a government this week.
The opposition has threatened nationwide protests and a general strike if parliament votes for a new Socialist cabinet. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
